walkthroughs.body_html:
An Introduction to Christian Ethics — a core area of GCSE Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

An Introduction to Christian Ethics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with An Introduction to Christian Ethics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What is the second formulation about?
options: Universalisability
Humanity as end
Kingdom of ends
Good will

mcqs.q: What does the cosmological argument try to prove?
options: The cosmological argument proves the Big Bang happened.
Atman and Brahman are two competing Hindu gods.
The cosmological argument proves who created life on Earth.
That the existence of the universe requires a first cause or necessary being — usually identified with God — to explain why anything exists at all.

mcqs.q: What do Christians mean by resurrection, and how does it differ from reincarnation?
options: Atman and Brahman are two competing Hindu gods.
Christians believe everyone is reincarnated until they accept Jesus.
Resurrection and reincarnation are basically the same idea of life after death.

Resurrection is the once-for-all bodily raising to eternal life at the end of time (modelled on Christ's resurrection); reincarnation is the soul's repeated rebirth into new bodies. They are distinct doctrines from different religious traditions.
